value.overview: The Spectacled Owl (Pulsatrix perspicillata) is a large, powerful owl of the tropical Americas. It is named for the broad pale markings that surround its yellow eyes and contrast with its dark facial disk. This mainly nocturnal species inhabits forested landscapes and hunts from concealed perches. Although usually solitary or found in pairs, it can be locally conspicuous because of its deep, far-carrying calls. Costa Rica supports resident populations across both Caribbean and Pacific slopes.
value.classification: The Spectacled Owl belongs to the owl order Strigiformes and the typical owl family Strigidae. It is the largest member of the genus Pulsatrix, which includes several large forest owls of the Neotropics.
value.identification: Adults are large owls with dark brown upperparts, a blackish facial disk, bold whitish or buff eye markings, a white throat, and finely barred brown underparts. The eyes are yellow, and the bill is pale horn-colored. Juveniles are mostly white and fluffy, with a dark face and barred wings. Its size, conspicuous spectacles, white throat, and broad rounded wings help distinguish it from smaller Costa Rican owls. It is more often heard than seen at night.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central and South America to southern Brazil and northern Argentina, including Trinidad. In Costa Rica it is a widespread resident on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, from lowlands to about 1,500 meters in suitable areas. It uses mature and secondary forest, forest edges, gallery forest, cacao plantations, wooded savannas, and other landscapes with substantial tree cover. Dense vegetation near rivers may provide important roosting habitat, while large trees are needed for nesting.
value.migrationStatus: The Spectacled Owl is generally sedentary and resident throughout its range. In Costa Rica it occurs year-round, with no regular long-distance migration known. Local movements may occur when birds forage, disperse, or respond to changes in food and habitat.
value.breeding: Spectacled Owls usually nest in spacious natural cavities in large trees rather than building open nests. The clutch commonly contains about two eggs, although reproductive details can vary among regions. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported during the dry season and into the early rainy season. The female generally incubates while the male supplies food. Young birds remain dependent on their parents for an extended period and may stay with them for many months after leaving the nest.
value.dietFeeding: This owl is a versatile carnivore. Its prey includes rodents and other small mammals, bats, birds, reptiles, amphibians, large insects, and occasionally other available animals. It commonly hunts at night from a high, quiet perch, watching for movement before dropping or gliding down to seize prey. Its broad diet allows it to use both intact forest and some human-modified habitats, provided adequate cover and prey remain available.
value.behavior: Spectacled Owls are primarily nocturnal, spending the day concealed in dense foliage or other sheltered sites. They are usually solitary or found as mated pairs and defend territories with deep hoots and other vocalizations. At dusk and during the night they move between elevated perches while hunting. They may use forest edges and clearings for foraging but generally depend on wooded areas for roosting, nesting, and protection.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, but the species is not currently assessed as globally threatened.
